home.name: Red Gabriel G. Tagura
home.role: 4th Year CS Student — Systems Programming & Backend Engineering
bio: Most of my projects start with the same question: what's actually happening underneath? That curiosity drove me to engineer a zero-dependency HTTP/1.1 engine from scratch in Zig. Focusing on building lean, high-concurrency systems that run close to the metal.
Currently pursuing a Bachelor of Science in Computer Science at the Polytechnic University of the Philippines - Manila.
This site is served by a custom HTTP/1.1 server written in Zig, using epoll and POSIX I/O directly. No libuv, no framework. The simplest thing that could possibly work at scale.

items.name: Stratified Autonomous Memory Manager
items.subtitle: Undergraduate Thesis
desc: Developing an offline profile-guided allocator in Zig using mmap with K-Means lifetime prediction to pre-bake arena selection, aiming to reduce P99 latency and peak RSS in the Node.js heap on 1 GB-constrained backend services.

items.name: r-alloc
items.subtitle: Custom Memory Allocator
desc: Arena and slab allocators in C++ on mmap, chosen per call site by a small lifetime model and bridged to Node.js with N-API to bypass V8's garbage collector: 43.5% lower peak RSS than V8 (74.5 vs 132 MB over about a million operations) and about 30% lower worst-case latency, at a 16% throughput cost.

items.name: Ambigui2
items.subtitle: Quantum Tetris AI
items.tags: Zig · Raylib · Expectimax · CMA-ES · Genetic Algorithm · WebAssembly
desc: Tetris in superposition: every piece is two tetrominoes at once and collapses into one when it lands. A bitboard engine in Zig (one u16 per row) does a collision check in 3.8 ns and a line clear in 16 ns, and the search visits ~2M positions/s on one core. Runs on desktop, in a terminal, and in the browser as a ~0.5 MB WebAssembly build.

Expectimax AI with hold search, beam pruning, and a transposition table; its evaluation weights are learned by self-play with a genetic algorithm and a from-scratch CMA-ES, chosen on held-out games. The reworked Hard AI clears 105 lines per game vs 43.5 before (2.4×), at 8.2 ms per move vs 21.7 (2.7× faster).

posts.title: Writing an HTTP/1.1 server in Zig from scratch
posts.excerpt: How I replaced a framework-backed server with 600 lines of Zig, raw POSIX sockets, and Linux epoll. What the syscall boundary looks like, where memory gets tricky, and why the binary is around 300 KB.

posts.title: My first ever project
posts.excerpt: The smooth journey of our group in learning the fundamentals of software development using Java Swing and Java. No backend frameworks.

paragraphs: This site is served by a custom HTTP/1.1 server written in Zig 0.15.2. It uses Linux epoll for I/O readiness and raw POSIX system calls for file serving — no libuv, no Tokio, no libevent. One thread, one event loop, about 800 lines of Zig and a build.zig.

Stripped, the binary is about 310 KB. It speaks keep-alive, drops connections that sit idle for 60 seconds, and sends a real Content-Length on every response. Static files, plus /health and /stats endpoints. It runs on a Microsoft Azure B2ats v2 VM behind Caddy.
